concepts.title: A House Whispering for Money
concepts.definition: D.H. Lawrence opens on a genteel house with a subtle secret: it is haunted by the unspoken phrase 'there must be more money'. The parents, handsome and genteel, have no luck -- the mother Hester feels her loveless marriage and her children's questioning eyes -- and the children hear the walls whisper their need.
concepts.key_idea: Greed as a haunting -- a house that whispers what its owners never say aloud.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww103.txt opening sections (house whispering there must be more money, hester the mother, luck versus money, loveless household)
question_patterns: what did the children hear whispering in the house

solution_steps.explain: The phrase 'there must be more money' runs through the house though nobody says it aloud -- greed unspoken but omnipresent.
Hester cannot love her children, and luck -- not money -- is what she says she lacks, confusing the two for her son.
Paul takes the burden on himself: if luck brings money, he will find luck to stop the voices.

concepts.title: Paul's Rocking-horse and the Winning Secrets
concepts.definition: Paul discovers that riding his rocking-horse furiously, in a trance, delivers the names of race winners -- he 'knows' by luck, he says. With gardener Bassett and uncle Oscar he bets, wins, and secretly banks money, even sending his mother a thousand pounds a year anonymously on her birthday -- yet the house only screams louder.
concepts.key_idea: A boy rides a toy toward fortune -- and every gift only feeds the hunger it was meant to silence.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww103.txt rocking horse sections (paul rides the rocking horse, bassett the gardener, uncle oscar, winning bets, birthday gift of thousand pounds)
question_patterns: how does paul claim to know the winners of races

solution_steps.explain: Paul rocks the horse wildly, eyes fixed, until the name of the next winner arrives to him.
With Bassett holding the money and Uncle Oscar joining, Paul's predictions pile up a secret fortune.
The anonymous birthday gift makes the flowers and letters scream louder -- money multiplies the appetite it feeds.

concepts.title: The Final Ride and the Theme of Destructive Desire
concepts.definition: To silence the house Paul rides his horse through the night before the Derby, falls ill with brain fever after shouting the winner's name -- Malabar. He wins eighty thousand pounds, but dies that night. Lawrence's theme stands complete: the hunger for money, especially money bought for love, destroys the lover and the loved alike.
concepts.key_idea: The horse rides to death -- love replaced by luck, luck paid for with a child's life.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww103.txt climax sections (derby night ride, malabar, brain fever, paul's death, uncle oscar's final words, theme of money and love)

solution_steps.explain: Paul rocks through the feverish night until he collapses, crying the Derby winner's name -- Malabar.
The bet wins eighty thousand pounds, delivered to a dying boy who never hears his mother say she is lucky.
Lawrence indicts a values-system where love is measured in money -- the whispering house wins, the child loses.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the difference between luck and money as the story presents it, using the mother's answers to Paul.

solution_template.explain: Asked why they are poor, Hester answers that it is because they have no luck, not merely no money.
Paul concludes that luck causes money, so being lucky is the way to give his mother what the house wants.
Her careless distinction becomes the boy's fatal mission -- the miscommunication drives the plot.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Comment on the irony of Paul's final victory in the Derby.

solution_template.explain: The same night brings the winning name Malabar and Paul's collapse into brain fever.
Eighty thousand pounds arrive to a boy who is dying -- the goal achieved precisely as its purpose fails.
The irony indicts the desire itself: money won to purchase love arrives when nothing can be purchased any more.
